gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1024r:
Financial Audits, GAO-05-1024R of September 30, 2005, maps which parts of the executive branch must have their books checked each year. The Chief Financial Officers Act of 1990 set that duty for 24 major departments and agencies. The Accountability of Tax Dollars Act of 2002 spread it to most of the rest. Waivers could free some small units.

Congress asked GAO to find any units left outside the net. GAO also listed units that won a waiver for fiscal years 2003 and 2004, with their budget sums. The text packs the June 27, 2005 staff briefing into report form, for use in budget oversight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1034r:
Federally Chartered Corporation, GAO-05-1034R of September 30, 2005, reports GAO's read of the audit of the National Federation of Music Clubs. The federation holds a federal charter. It was set up to spur American musical work. Law at 36 U.S.C. 10101 makes such groups file a yearly audit with Congress, and GAO reviews each one.

The audit here covers fiscal year 2003. Auditors said the books were fairly shown on a modified cash basis of accounting. GAO found no case of rule-breaking worth a report. The short letter gives the scope of the read and that clean outcome in full.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1044r:
Nuclear Cleanup, GAO-05-1044R of September 22, 2005, sends early results from a review of the Rocky Flats closure near Denver. For about 40 years, the site made plutonium triggers for nuclear arms. The work left poison in its halls, soil, and water. Cleanup began in 1996 under a binding pact with state and federal watchdogs.

In 2001, GAO saw the job over cost and behind plan. Now the hired firm plans to end the hands-on work early and under budget. GAO asks what drove the gain. It asks the end date and full cost, plus how crews will prove the site is safe.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-504r:
A short GAO letter, GAO-05-504R of June 10, 2005, deals with the General Federation of Women's Clubs and its fiscal year ended June 30, 2003. The federation links women's clubs and like groups around the world. It advances their shared interests in education, work, charity, letters, art, and science.

The review follows the standard pattern for chartered corporations. The law calls for yearly financial statements with real detail on income and spending. It also calls for an audit by an independent public accountant. GAO read the statements and the auditor's report and tested the figures with basic analysis. Its charge was to tell the House Judiciary Committee about any reporting lapse. It found no lapse that had to be reported. The auditor held the statements to be fairly presented under generally accepted accounting principles. The audit reports were returned with the letter.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-584r:
Moves from political posts into career jobs across government are counted in a GAO letter, GAO-05-584R, dated June 9, 2005. A conversion happens when a worker changes status without a break in service over 3 days. One kind shifts a person from a noncareer post into a career one. Such moves must meet the rules and the job's qualification standards. GAO asked 41 departments and agencies to report their counts.

The letter covers a 32-month span, from May 1, 2001, through December 31, 2003. It lists how many workers each body converted in that window. Its methods section lists the kinds of posts covered and the tests used to pick the 41 bodies. A fuller study was promised for a later date. That study will span 4 years, through April 30, 2005. It will add traits of each conversion and a closer look at how the moves were made. This letter is the head count; the judgment comes later.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-594r:
In GAO report GAO-05-594R (June 23, 2005), the Education Department's fiscal year 2004 representation letter comes under review. The letter confirms, for the government-wide audit, what department leaders told their auditors about the year's financial statements. GAO checked it against five key areas. Three of the five showed weaknesses that GAO asked the department to repair.

Materiality thresholds were missing, as in most letters this cycle. The letter included 25 of the 29 standard representations that applied to the department. Two more were partial, and 2 were absent. The summary of misstatements left uncorrected was incomplete as well. It did not distinguish errors touching other agencies' accounts from errors touching the public's. GAO made three recommendations to the chief financial officer, each tied to a specific change. It also recommended that the inspector general work with the department on the letters that follow.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-604r:
The General Services Administration's fiscal year 2004 representation letter closes this group as GAO-05-604R, a letter dated July 14, 2005. The letter, addressed to the agency's chief financial officer and its inspector general, forms part of the record for the audit of the government's financial statements. GAO reviewed the letter against the standard conditions in the federal audit manual.

One defect heads the findings: the letter did not include a complete summary of unadjusted misstatements. Such a summary tells auditors which known errors management chose not to correct, and how large they are. Without it, the government-wide audit loses a check on the agency's figures. The report sets out conclusions and recommendations for executive action on the point. Enclosures list the standard representations the audit manual expects and carry the finance office's comments, with GAO's reply. The letter is a narrow but telling piece of the fiscal year 2004 audit record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-814r:
A large bookkeeping error at the State Department is audited in GAO-05-814R, dated September 20, 2005. Many agencies had to restate their fiscal year 2003 accounts to fix errors. Such fixes can shake public trust. GAO must audit the government's joined accounts each year. This letter looks at what went wrong at State and why its auditor missed it.

GAO found two large entries were recorded badly. Together they made up most of a $927 million error. Managers failed to review the entries well enough to catch the fault. The outside auditor's tests were not built to catch this kind of entry error. GAO told State's finance chief to test new review steps. It told the inspector general to make sure future audit tests can catch like errors.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-864r:
Privacy notices for an airline screening program are judged in GAO-05-864R, a letter dated July 22, 2005. The Secure Flight program checks passenger data against terror watch lists. To test it, the security agency used data from private firms as well as airlines. The Privacy Act requires open notice of such uses. GAO checked whether the agency's notices told the public the full story.

GAO found the fall 2004 notices fell short. The public was not fully told about the use of private data in testing. Nor could the public comment on it in time. Notices filed in September 2004 and November 2004 left out steps for gathering and using the data. The title adds the turn: the agency has lately taken steps to inform the public more fully.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-124r:
A funding violation at the Department of Veterans Affairs is found in GAO-06-124R, a letter report dated November 30, 2005. VA serves about 4.7 million veterans through hospitals, clinics, and nursing homes. To cut costs, VA studies whether private firms should run parts of its operations. The law bars VA from paying for such cost comparison studies with health care funds. Congress must make those funds available for studies by name. GAO checked whether VA obeyed that bar.

GAO concluded that VA broke the purpose statute. It paid for some studies with Veterans Health Administration funds that were not open for that use. GAO made four recommendations to bring VA into line with the funding bar. VA disagreed with the reading of the law and rejected the recommendations. It argued the bar covers only one type of study. GAO stood by its reading and its findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-194r:
Test access for students with disabilities is the topic of GAO-06-194R, a letter report dated October 28, 2005. The National Assessment of Educational Progress is known as the Nation's Report Card. It tracks student achievement over time and across states. In July 2005 GAO reported that most states include students with disabilities in state tests. For this letter, GAO turned to the national test's own data. It measured how often such students were kept out of the test.

Working with Education Department officials, GAO read the 2002 data closely. The reading showed that 5 percent of students with disabilities were excluded from the 2002 reading test. Exclusion rates matter because a test that skips these students tells a skewed story. The letter adds the national figures to the state picture from the earlier report. It helps readers judge how full the nation's report card really is.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-254r:
The Agriculture Department's restated books are the subject of GAO-06-254R, a letter report dated January 25, 2006. The department had to redo part of its fiscal year 2003 consolidated statements to fix errors. The case arose in GAO's audit of the government's own books for fiscal year 2004. That audit found a growing line of agencies restating past figures. This letter, one of a series, gives GAO's findings on the department's restatement.

GAO made three recommendations. Two go to the department's finance chief. He must make sure the steps meant to stop like errors are truly in place. He must also watch how audit results and restatements get shown in future years. The third goes to the inspector general, who must see that audit tests catch wrongly booked appropriations. Clear disclosure matters, GAO noted, since a muddy note can mislead a reader of the statements. The letter guards trust in the corrected figures.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-384r:
Sick and injured soldiers were still being paid as if they faced hostile fire. A GAO letter report, GAO-06-384R of April 27, 2006, investigates pay at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. The claim began with 37 Army Guard and Reserve soldiers in a medical unit. They were said to get hostile fire and hardship duty pay while in outpatient status. The title puts the wider count at over 200 soldiers.

GAO tested whether the claim was true and how far the problem spread. It also traced the causes and the effect on soldiers and families. GAO blamed inadequate controls for stopping the overpayments. Readers get the scope, causes, and human cost.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-424r:
One word, insurance, turns out to have no single shared meaning. A GAO letter, GAO-06-424R of February 23, 2006, reports on definitions of insurance. GAO briefed congressional staff on early results on June 24, 2005, and on final results on November 29, 2005. The letter covers the search for a universal definition and the problems in that search.

GAO lists parts that commonly appear in definitions. It names products not defined or regulated the same way across states. It weighs effects of split definitions by risk type. It also covers new work on risk transfer in reinsurance. Readers see why one definition is hard to set.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-504r:
Chemists' national society is a federally chartered corporation with audited books. Letter GAO-06-504R, dated March 14, 2006, reviews the American Chemical Society audits. The reports cover fiscal years ended December 31, 2003 and 2002. The society works to advance chemistry and promote research in chemical science and industry. It spreads chemical knowledge through meetings, reports, papers, and publications.

GAO read the financial statements and the auditors' reports. Its aim was to flag any failure to meet the law's reporting rules. GAO found no reportable instance of noncompliance. The auditors said the statements were presented fairly. They followed U.S. generally accepted accounting principles. Readers get a short, clean audit review.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-684r:
In GAO-06-684R (May 12, 2006), GAO reviewed the outside audit of the Paralyzed Veterans of America for fiscal years 2003 and 2002. The group speaks for veterans with spinal cord wounds and disease. It holds a federal charter. The law says chartered groups must put out yearly financial statements. The statements must show what they own, what they owe, what came in, and what went out. An outside public accountant must audit them.

GAO read the audit reports and the statements they covered. GAO found no cases it had to report in which the group broke the law's rules for yearly statements. The outside auditor held that the statements were fairly shown in line with United States generally accepted accounting principles. GAO's short letter puts that clean result on record for Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-754r:
Export limits on powerful computers are at issue in GAO-06-754R, a letter report GAO issued on June 30, 2006. The United States controls exports of high performance computers for security and foreign policy reasons. These machines serve both civilian and military uses. A performance threshold decides which exports need a license. The President must justify changes to that threshold under the National Defense Authorization Act of 1998.

GAO is required by law to assess such proposed changes. GAO weighed foreign availability of similar machines and the security risks of the new threshold. GAO found that the President's justification did not fully address the 1998 law's requirements. Gaps remained on the points the law demands. The letter keeps Congress informed on a quiet but sensitive trade control.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-794r:
Care as troops move from war service to veteran status is reviewed in GAO-06-794R, a letter report dated June 30, 2006. By the end of March 2006, over 1.3 million servicemembers had served in the Afghanistan and Iraq operations. Many may seek care from the Department of Veterans Affairs during duty or after leaving service. The two departments aimed to make that handoff seamless. GAO reported on their joint efforts.

GAO described a wide range of outreach by the veterans agency. From October 1, 2000, through May 31, 2006, it gave about 36,000 briefings to almost 1.4 million troops and family audiences. The briefings explained health services that may be open to them. GAO also tracked how the agencies share records and coordinate care. The letter shows a system straining to welcome a new veteran generation.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-924r:
Two years of accounts for the Congressional Medal of Honor Society are covered by GAO letter GAO-06-924R, dated July 7, 2006. The society guards the honor of the Medal, shields its holders from misuse, and fosters love of country. Its federal charter brings a duty to file audited statements.

The audit reports span the fiscal years that ended December 31, 2004 and 2003. GAO read those reports as the charter law directs. The auditor found the statements fairly shown, in line with U.S. accounting rules. GAO saw no breach worth a report. The letter closes the audit check for those two years.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1234r:
Some exports can serve both military and civilian users, from trucks to aircraft services. A GAO letter, GAO-07-1234R, dated September 27, 2007, reports on Export-Import Bank financing of such dual-use exports. Since October 1994, the bank may fund them only if they are nonlethal and mainly for civilian use. Law requires GAO to report each year on how the financed items were used. This letter covers fiscal year 2005 and adds data back to 2002.

The bank financed no dual-use export projects in fiscal year 2005. It has considered no new requests since then, officials told GAO. The last such financing was in fiscal year 2002. That year the bank backed four projects totaling $24.6 million. The letter's enclosure lists the 2002 projects and the end-use checks the bank ran on them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-194r:
Head Start buses carry some of the nation's poorest children to preschool. A GAO letter, GAO-07-194R, dated November 17, 2006, adds detail on bus safety rules. The rules took effect in 2001 and require school buses or like vehicles. They also require child restraints and a monitor on board. Congress asked GAO to compare programs that struggled with the rules to those that did not. About 900,000 children take part in Head Start.

A little less than a third of programs offering transport reported challenges, GAO found. Those programs ran more centers and more buses each day. They were also more likely to hire a school system to drive. By March 2006, 378 programs had asked for more time to meet two of the rules. Those programs carried almost 75,000 children. That was about 22 percent of all Head Start children transported. It builds on GAO's July 2006 study.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-294r:
Universities bill the health institutes for lab space and support staff on top of direct research costs. GAO reviewed that overhead stream in GAO-07-294R, dated January 31, 2007. The institutes spend over 80 percent of a budget above $28 billion on outside research. More than 500 universities share the work. GAO tracked indirect cost trends for fiscal years 2003 through 2005. It also checked audits and follow-up on bad claims.

Indirect costs held steady at about 28.5 percent of grant funds, GAO found. The dollar total rose from about $3.9 billion to about $4.3 billion. Rates stay fixed for 2 to 4 years once set. About 390 of some 530 universities needed yearly single audits. The inspector general audited only about 4 schools a year. Follow-up on questioned costs was partial. Of $1.5 million questioned in reviewed files, the institutes recovered $864,860. That is about 56 percent of the sum.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-324r: Vietnam Veterans of America holds a federal charter, and GAO reviews the audits of such groups. GAO-07-324R, dated January 26, 2007, reports GAO's review of the group's outside audit. The audit covered fiscal year 2005. The auditors held that the group's statements were presented fairly under standard accounting rules. GAO's review found no breaches worth reporting. The letter is part of GAO's standing watch over chartered groups.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-34r:
The main report on a sole-source embassy security deal faults both the award and the billing. GAO issued it as GAO-07-34R on November 8, 2006. The State Department's contract has a $354 million ceiling. A joint venture installs alarms, cameras, and access gear at embassies. A fraud hotline tip opened the review. GAO studied the award basis, travel billing, and contract oversight. A companion letter covers the small business agency's role.

The award relied on an unauthorized blanket waiver, GAO found. Fixed-price travel billing then overpaid the firm. One task priced 23 travelers for Baghdad work. Only 10 actually traveled. The government paid $380,000 above real costs on that task. Reviewers checked technical plans but not traveler counts. A new clause lets the government claw back unused travel funds. It had not yet been used when GAO wrote.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-414r:
The cost of fixing the United Nations headquarters in New York keeps climbing, and GAO-07-414R, dated February 15, 2007, tracks the rise. The UN's Capital Master Plan would bring the complex up to current safety and building codes. It would also meet security and technology needs. The United States, as host and top funder, has a large stake in the work.

The UN Secretary-General's latest estimate put the price at $1.88 billion. That was about $128 million above the 2005 figure. GAO broke down what drove the increase. It also reported the General Assembly's latest choices on scope, schedule, and funding. The report closes with the share the United States would pay.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-474r:
American music gets a boost from the National Federation of Music Clubs, and GAO-07-474R, issued March 9, 2007, reviews the federation's audit. The group promotes American music in the United States and abroad. It holds a federal charter, so it must file yearly financial statements in set detail. It must also obtain an audit by an outside public accountant.

GAO's letter covers the fiscal year ended June 30, 2004. Staff read the audit report, the statements, and the notes. They ran checks on the figures but did not perform an audit of their own. The review found no reportable breach of the law's reporting terms. One point sets this letter apart from its peers: the auditor's opinion rested on a modified cash basis of accounting, not the standard accrual rules. The statements were held fairly presented on that basis.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-514r:
How two Pacific nations spent their U.S. sector grants is detailed in GAO-07-514R, a short GAO supplement dated May 25, 2007. It adds to a December 2006 report on the amended Compacts of Free Association. The main report warned that the Federated States of Micronesia and the Republic of the Marshall Islands face hard tests in planning for lasting self-support. This letter covers grant use from 2004 through 2006.

The surviving text centers on the education sector grants. It sets out the goals and terms for each nation's education funding. Those goals stress quality basic education, higher student achievement, and teacher training. They also call for better management and tighter accountability. Funding levels and hurdles for each nation get their own sections. Extra supplemental education grants close the account. The letter is a data annex more than a verdict.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-554r:
Two health systems share patients but not always their drug lists, and GAO-07-554R, dated April 30, 2007, tracks the fix. Since 1998, the Defense Department and the Department of Veterans Affairs have worked to swap patient data by computer. Shared patients see doctors in both systems. A full drug list from both sides helps clinicians spot bad drug mixes and allergies.

In March 2004 the pair began a push to make pharmacy data computable. That means data a program can act on, such as auto-checking for harmful reactions. GAO found that computable drug data now flow for some shared patients. Gaps remain for the rest. The letter sets out what each agency expects the swap to prevent. It then gives the status of the build. The goal is plain: no clinician should prescribe blind to the other system's chart.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-664r:
Medical training has a chartered fund raiser, and its audit is cleared in GAO-07-664R, a GAO letter dated April 5, 2007. The National Fund for Medical Education raises private money for medical training. It hands out those funds, reads the field's needs, and works to improve how medical staff are trained. As a federally chartered corporation, it must file yearly financial statements and obtain an outside audit under 36 U.S.C. 10101.

GAO reviewed the audit report for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2004. Staff read the statements and the notes and ran checks on the figures. GAO did not audit the fund itself and gave no opinion of its own. The review found no reportable breach of the law's reporting rules. The auditor's opinion held that the statements were fairly presented under U.S. accounting standards. The letter is one of a spring batch of charter reviews.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-694r:
Medicaid waiver deals in Florida and Vermont are covered by GAO-07-694R, a letter GAO issued on July 24, 2007. Medicaid gives health cover to about 60 million low-income people. Under section 1115 of the Social Security Act, the Health and Human Services chief can waive some rules for test projects. Florida and Vermont won such deals for most of their programs. GAO checked what the deals mean for patients. It also checked whether the public got a say before approval.

Florida's plan, launched in July 2006, makes many patients pick a managed care plan. Plans compete by offering distinct sets of benefits. Vermont took a distinct path to run its program. As of March 2007, both plans were too new to judge their effects on patients. GAO found the old concern still stands. The public had too little chance to weigh in while federal officials weighed the deals.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-704r:
Mine inspector hiring at the Mine Safety and Health Administration is covered in GAO-07-704R, a letter dated May 16, 2007. In 2003, GAO told the agency to plan for a wave of inspector retirements. This letter reports follow-up work done from June 2006 to March 2007. GAO read the agency's workforce plans and hiring data. It spoke with human resource staff and district officials. The core question was whether hiring reforms had worked.

A new hiring path, the Federal Career Intern Program, began in 2004. It helped the agency spot skilled applicants early. It also cut the time needed to hire. The agency took on 236 new coal mine inspector trainees under the program. The gains did not fix the long view, though. Over 40 percent of inspectors could retire by 2012. District chiefs feared losing seasoned staff would slow safety checks. GAO found the agency's workforce plan did not project or meet that need well.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-834r:
Answers to follow-up questions on improper payments form GAO-07-834R, a letter dated May 30, 2007. On March 29, 2007, GAO testified to a Senate panel on payment errors. The hearing covered the Improper Payments Information Act of 2002. It also covered the Recovery Auditing Act in a 2002 defense law. Congress sent written questions on April 18, 2007. This letter answers them. It rests on past GAO work and agency reports.

The answers track agency reporting from fiscal years 2004 through 2006. They cover trends in how much error agencies report. They also cover blocks to sound reporting and tighter controls. Recovery audits, which claw back overpayments to contractors, get their own answers. Agencies must find programs at risk of large errors each year. They must estimate the sums and report repair plans. The letter gives Congress the detail behind GAO's hearing claims.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1054r:
A plan to move a command center from a mountain site is revisited in GAO letter GAO-08-1054R, dated September 18, 2008. In July 2006, commanders said they would move some North American Aerospace Defense Command functions from Cheyenne Mountain. The new home would be a joint center at Peterson Air Force Base in Colorado.

GAO warned in May 2007 that the move lacked study of its effects, costs, and risks. Congress then ordered a defense report on the shift. This letter presses the two commands to reevaluate the risks of the new site. It also asks them to state in plain terms that they accept those risks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-244r:
A base saved by a new mission is reviewed in GAO letter GAO-08-244R of January 18, 2008. In September 2005, the closure commission voted to shut Cannon Air Force Base in New Mexico. The base could stay open only if a new mission arrived by the end of 2009. In June 2006, the Air Force gave it the special operations command. The command took ownership on October 1, 2007.

The letter explains what drove that choice. It gives the cost estimate and timeline for moving staff in. Extra costs fell outside the closure process, GAO notes. Congress never weighed them when it let the closure plan stand. GAO gives lawmakers a point to ponder for future rounds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-274r:
New border document rules are observed in GAO letter GAO-08-274R of December 20, 2007. For years, travelers from Canada, Bermuda, and parts of the hemisphere entered with a driver's license or birth certificate. Some showed nothing at all. Such papers are easy to fake. A 2004 law requires a passport or a like proof of identity and citizenship for entry from the region.

Since May 2006, two departments have moved the plan forward. They chose which documents will count and began formal rule making. A new passport card is in design for land crossings. Training staff and teaching the public remain large tasks. The letter gauges the pace.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-354r:
The Army's Grow the Force funding plan is reviewed in GAO letter GAO-08-354R, dated January 18, 2008. The plan would grow the Army from 1,037,000 to 1,112,000 soldiers by fiscal year 2013, adding six active brigade combat teams and support units. The Army put the added cost at about $70.2 billion through that year.

GAO found the plan neither transparent nor complete. Budget papers did not show how the cost figures were built, and some costs were left out, including over $2.5 billion for health care and education support tied to the added troops. A later move to speed the growth to fiscal year 2010 could raise costs further. Without fuller figures, GAO said, lawmakers cannot weigh the plan against other defense needs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-444r:
Defense Travel System payment checks are questioned in GAO letter GAO-08-444R, dated March 3, 2008. The letter grew out of GAO's work on the Defense Department's fiscal year 2006 report under the Improper Payments Information Act of 2002. That work covered travel spending across the department.

For fiscal year 2006, the department reported about $8 million in bad travel payments, near 1 percent of reported travel payments. But the data behind that figure covered only payments run through the Defense Travel System, about 10 percent of the $8.5 billion in travel obligations that year. The estimate also left out the Army, the system's biggest user, which GAO says would likely add over $4 million. The sampling method itself was flawed, so the figures were not statistically valid. The department agreed with three of GAO's four recommendations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-454r:
National Institutes of Health research on jaw disorders is surveyed in GAO letter GAO-08-454R, dated April 4, 2008. Temporomandibular joint and muscle disorders cause pain in the jaw joint and nearby muscles, and in a few people they bring lasting pain and lost jaw function. Their causes are often unknown, which makes diagnosis and treatment hard.

From fiscal year 2002 through fiscal year 2006, NIH backed 170 projects tied to these disorders. Most ran through the National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research, with nine other institutes and centers also taking part. The work ranged over how common the disorders are, what triggers them, sex differences, pain, and jaw mechanics. Officials said future support will follow merit review and targeted funding calls, several of which ran from December 2005 through December 2007.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-474r:
Health savings accounts are updated in GAO letter GAO-08-474R, dated April 1, 2008. Since 2004, these tax-advantaged accounts pair with high-deductible health plans. GAO first reported on users in 2006 and now refreshes the data on who takes part and how they use the accounts.

Coverage under these plans jumped from about 438,000 people in September 2004 to about 4.5 million by January 2007, still only about 2 percent of private coverage in 2006. Yet over 40 percent of enrollees in these plans never opened an account. Tax filers reporting account activity in 2005 averaged about $139,000 in income, against about $57,000 for other filers. Contributions reported in 2005 totaled $754 million, about twice the $366 million withdrawn.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-544r:
Evacuation planning for people without transport is tracked in GAO letter GAO-08-544R, dated April 1, 2008. About 100,000 people did not leave before Hurricane Katrina struck in 2005, and the storm killed over 1,300. Many lacked a car. Hospitals and nursing homes also struggled to move patients.

This letter reports the status of GAO's past advice. A 2006 federal review found only about 10 percent of state plans and about 12 percent of urban plans handled these evacuations well. One city GAO visited expected few to need help, though census data showed 16.5 percent of its households had no car. Liability fears keep some transport firms from helping. GAO urged clearer federal roles and required local readiness. Both departments agreed to consider the advice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-704r:
How many cargo planes the military needs is a costly call. Law for fiscal year 2008 ordered a study, done by an outside research center, on the right size and mix for the airlift fleet. GAO-08-704R, a letter dated April 28, 2008, judges the draft plan for that study.

The draft plan is too thin to judge, GAO says. It skips parts the law names, such as the assumptions the study will use, and lacks gauges of success. With no clear thread back to the law, no one can tell if the study will be fair or complete. GAO told the Defense Department to make sure the final plan has that detail.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-864r:
A tiny board that probes chemical accidents gets a management review in GAO-08-864R, a letter dated August 22, 2008. The Chemical Safety Board began work in 1998, with $9.4 million and 39 staff for fiscal year 2008. It has no power to punish, only to find causes and urge fixes.

The board heard of about 900 chemical accidents in calendar year 2007 and took 31 grave or deadly ones for full probes. Watchdogs have given it 32 fix proposals since fiscal year 2001, spanning accountability, staffing, and legal duties. The letter says management and oversight still need work, echoing a GAO review from 2000.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-884r:
Roadside bombs cause about 75 percent of U.S. combat losses in Iraq and Afghanistan. Blast-proof trucks, called MRAPs, were rushed to the field to cut those deaths. GAO-08-884R, a letter dated July 15, 2008, describes the fast-track buying method and the hurdles left.

More than $22 billion has been given to buy over 15,000 vehicles, and about 6,600 were fielded by mid-2008. The program kept demands minimal, used off-the-shelf designs, and built, tested, and shipped at the same time. Nine vendors won open-ended deals for up to 4,100 vehicles a year each. Top priority status sped the work across industry.
